chapter_theme: The last songs at Chidambaram (புலியூர்): courtesans who take a man's wealth, the body as a pot of filth for dogs and flies, and the slide from lust to old age, death and the burning ground; against these the poet asks for teaching in the meaning of Siva's emblems, for release, for the yogic ascent through the letters of the five-syllable mantra, and he speaks to his own mind.
structure_note: 509, 512, 514 and 516 confess women; 510 and 512 dwell on the body's foulness and end; 511 is a yogic plea; 513 is addressed to the poet's mind; 515 is a litany with no plea. 516 ends at Kunruthoradal, not at Chidambaram.

509.reading: The poet asks not to be confused by courtesans who cast nets with their earrings, garlanded hair and lip-nectar, nor by their songs, their scheming life, youth and lust for gold; he asks for the day when he will be taught what Siva's emblems mean: the skull-bowl, the holy ash, the konrai in the matted hair, the axe and the deer, and the primal origin. The praise identifies Murugan with the sage who with the sword of knowledge defeated the hair-plucking Jains and sang the Veda as songs, and names the dance shown in turn to the serpent-form sage and the tiger sage of Puliyur, amid drum syllables, ghouls and Kali's host.
509.nuance: The plea is unusual: not for the feet but for உபதேசம், teaching on what Siva's ornaments signify (இவையிவை என). தலைபறி அமணர், the Jains who pluck their hair, and the sage who changed their community points to Sambandar, with whom the book identifies Murugan. அரிதுயில் சயன வியாளமூர்த்தன், the serpent on which Hari sleeps, is Patanjali as Adisesha. One word is corrupt.

510.reading: The poet calls his body a vessel of flesh, blood, bile and urine bound together, a rotting bed of pleasures, a worm-eaten life that becomes food for the tired ghoul, the dog and the fly, and asks Murugan to remove this pot and place him in that other one, granting release. The praise names Murugan at Puliyur who turns false anger to true anger and places devotees at his golden feet, and the son of Hara who took into service the hunter of the field, who offered green leaves and water from his mouth.
510.nuance: இக்கடத்தை நீக்கி அக்கடத்துள் ஆக்கி, remove this pot and make me within that pot, plays on கடம், pot or body: the second pot is the state of release. The leaves and the water carried in the mouth (பச்சிலை, வாய்க்குள் எச்சில்) are the marks of the hunter Kannappar's worship, which Hara accepted. Who the பொக்கணத்து நீற்றை இட்டு ... புனவேடன் is, Kannappar or Murugan as hunter, is not clear to me.

511.reading: A yogic plea: setting out the elements, the letters na, ma, si, va and ya at their places in the body, the cosmic sphere where the rays are stilled, the breath in its two channels, the purified senses, the sun and moon circles, the yantra, bindu and nada, the poet asks when he will reach that union. The praise is a battle in drum syllables with Vidyadharas, Tumburu and Narada singing and the Suras' bones and crowns scattered, and names the town that the serpent and the tiger saw.
511.nuance: நகர, மகர, சிகர, வகர, யகர are the five letters of நமசிவாய, set beside the elements (மண், கங்கை, மாருதம், ககனம்) as Tirumular sets them. The sequence is dense and I cannot follow every stage. உரகு உனும் புலி கண்ட ஊர் is Chidambaram as the place where Patanjali and Vyaghrapada saw the dance.

512.reading: The poet describes courtesans from hair to feet, who sell their breasts in the street, cheat and take a man's goods, and make love to him; caught in that infatuation he ruins his body, turns grey like a crane, loses sight and hearing, leaks filth, totters on a stick while people say 'chi chi', until Death takes his life, the corpse is dressed and named, drums are beaten, kin cry and beat their faces, and it is fed to the fire in the burning ground; he asks whether he must take up such sorrow daily. The praise names Siva who came as guru at the ford to take the horses and set his foot on the ascetic's head, the gods crying 'Kumara guru para', Vishnu's deeds as Narasimha, Vamana and Rama, and Murugan's embrace of the gypsy girl, at Puliyur.
512.nuance: The longest confession in these chapters, it runs without pause from the courtesans' trade (முலைவிலை உரைசெய்து, பொருள் பற்றி) to old age and the funeral, so that lust is shown leading straight to the burning ground. குருவின் உருவென ... குதிரை கொளவரு ... தவசி தலை பொற்பதம் வைத்து recalls the story of Manikkavasagar, for whom Siva came as guru and brought horses; the text gives its details, not the name.

513.reading: The poet speaks to his mind: 'Mind, come near and keep my word; I tell you what is good for you: worship the god of the peacock, king of his devotees, who gives the gods Siva's world and cuts the root of impurity, the supreme Brahman, our treasure and refuge.' The praise names Murugan as guru of Siva who sits with Kalyani, who took the Suras' heads while the ancients showered flowers, and who melts for the peacock-like Valli, at Tamil Puliyur.
513.nuance: The whole plea is addressed to மனமே, the mind as a separate party, as the lover speaks to his heart in love poetry; here the mind is urged toward worship rather than a beloved. மலநிலை வேர் அறுக்கவல, able to cut the root of the state of impurity, is Siddhanta language.

514.reading: The poet speaks of courtesans with parrot voices and pearl-hung breasts who seize a man's wealth and call in others, and asks that he, a dog caught in the net of deceitful women, be given knowledge and attainment on the seat of light, his whole mind gathered to Murugan's six, and be told the meaning with love. The praise names the vel that killed the Daityas of the seven islands, Murugan as son of Uma who is half of the dancing Lord, his embrace of the gypsy girl, and the husband of Indrani's daughter, at Puliyur.
514.nuance: பொருள் பற்றி வேறு அழைத்திடுவார், they take the wealth and call another, is the courtesan's trade. உனது ஆறினம் வைத்து may mean the six faces or the six-syllable mantra; the sense is uncertain.

515.reading: A litany with no plea, each line ending 'see, the Lord': the supreme guru who gives the state of teaching, the one exalted in the space of light without day or night, who rules the worlds, seen as Sivaya in earth, sky and elements, Uma's husband who rides the bull, the experience that has no end of ages, who ends the deeds and illusion that enter in the womb, the god of world-light who dances without ceasing in the golden hall.
515.nuance: Every epithet here belongs to Siva (உமைதன் மணவாளன், the dancer of கனகசபை), so the song either praises Siva or makes Murugan one with him; it does not say which. The refrain பெருமாள் காண் is unusual in the book. One word is corrupt.

516.reading: The poet speaks of courtesans with crores of deceit in their hearts, cooing and quarrelling, who bring desire, and asks not to waste away daily talking of love to breasts that bring the five great sins, but to be given the lotus feet the gods worship. The praise names the vel thrown at Sura to free the gods, Murugan as son of the konrai-wearer who danced with tinkling anklets, the supreme first, who dances on every hill.
516.nuance: பஞ்சமா பாவம் ஏதரு கொங்கை, breasts that bring the five great sins, puts lust among the gravest faults. The song ends at குன்றுதோறாடல், not at Chidambaram (see source_issues).

links.note: Both picture the body as food for scavengers: Naladiyar 48 has vultures tearing the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 510 the ghoul, the dog and the fly. The Naladiyar uses it to shame those who praise the body; 510 asks to be taken out of it into release.

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums (பறை), and both make the funeral a lesson: Naladiyar 24 notes that the dying carry the dead; 512 sets the funeral at the end of a life spent on courtesans.

Both speakers address their own mind (நெஞ்சே, மனமே) and urge it to set out with them on the good path. Naladiyar 55 gives the reason as youth wasted and old age coming; 513 gives only the Lord, who cuts the root of impurity.

source_issues: Song 509: one corrupt character in லு஡ட்டியும் (line 3); clearly ஊட்டியும்.
Song 515: one corrupt character in கருவுதனிலு஡று (line 13); clearly ஊறு.
Song 516: filed under சிதம்பரம் but ends at குன்றுதோறாடல் and names nothing of Chidambaram; the heading may be wrong.
